newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian government set for shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Russian government set for shake-up.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is poised to take a knife to his government after sharp criticism from President Boris Yeltsin and the appointment of liberal Kremlin aide Anatoly Chubais as first deputy premier.
The Kremlin and government were silent on Monday, however, as Russia took a public holiday to mark the March 8 Women's Day.
"We have no information," a Kremlin spokesman said when asked whether any announcement might be made on Monday. Chernomyrdin's press office was not answering the telephone.

Yeltsin, who declared "Enough is enough!" in a keynote speech on Thursday marking a dramatic return to the helm after illness, wants a major government shake-up to save his market reforms from collapsing amid corruption and popular despair.

The 66-year-old president took the first step in a widely leaked masterplan on the eve of the three-day holiday weekend, appointing Chubais, his liberal chief-of-staff, as first deputy prime minister late on Friday.

Kremlin sources say Chubais is likely to be sole number two to Chernomyrdin, with sweeping powers over the economy, and that three other first deputy prime ministers would be removed or demoted. The total number of deputy premiers may be cut to just a handful from the dozen named last August, the sources said.

First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin met the head of the state pension fund on Monday, Itar-Tass news agency said, according Ilyushin the rank he acquired when Chernomyrdin last rejigged his government just seven months ago.

Ilyushin was quoted as saying that a 50 to 60 percent shortfall in contributions to the state pension fund gathered by regional governments was "sabotage". Massive backlogs in pension payments, leaving millions of Russian with little or no income, is a major source of the discontent Yeltsin is now trying to head off.

It seems, however, that he has chosen the 41-year-old Chubais, an energetic and thick-skinned administrator for the task rather than the team Chernomyrdin put in place last summer after Yeltsin was re-elected. Chubais was appointed to chief aide in July after heading Yeltsin's campaign team.

He is respected in the West as a dedicated reformer, who during his previous spell in government, spearheaded "the sale of the century" in privatising much of Russia's Soviet-era economy. But the communist opposition hate him.
"Yeltsin should remember he is president of Russia, not of the IMF," communist parliamentary speaker Gennady Seleznyov said of Chubais' appointment. "People are just allergic to him."
That sort of reaction underlines how far Yeltsin, back in combative form after eight months out of action, considers the need to further reforms more important than opposition outrage.
Chubais and whatever new team is formed will have to act quickly, though. The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house formally voted to support a nationwide general strike for March 27.
The communists are threatening a no-confidence motion in the new government which, if voted through twice, would leave Yeltsin the choice of dismissing the cabinet or the Duma itself.
A fresh election might return an even less cooperative Duma in a country where, as Yeltsin himself admitted on Thursday, "people's patience has run out".
Despite the political risks, however, Western investors welcomed the appointment of Chubais.
"Foreign investment will be boosted by his appointment," Vlad Sobell of Daiwa Institute of Research said. "If anybody is going to deal with (speeding reform) it is going to be Chubais."
